transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose what brings me in is that for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always moving. I'm constantly puttering around, fixing things, arranging the house, or... or volunteering for just one more thing. It's just that, even at 87, I have a really hard time just sitting down and being still.
Has this need to stay busy always been a part of your personality, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

Well, I've always liked being active, but... this level of it is definitely more recent. It has been especially noticeable for about a year and five months now. That was right around the time I had a bunch of insurance bills and home repairs come up, and the stress of that just sort of pushed me into taking on more at the senior center. Ever since then, I just haven't been able to slow back down.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory or your ability to keep track of things lately?
Well, no, I haven't really noticed any changes there. My memory is still pretty sharp, thankfully. I don't have any trouble remembering things or keeping track of what I need to get done every day.
Over the past year, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless most of the time?

No, I haven't felt that way at all. I mean, I get a little stressed out sometimes, like with those home repairs I mentioned, but I certainly wouldn't say I've been depressed or hopeless. My mood is generally just fine.
Do you find that you spend a lot of your time worrying excessively about various everyday things, such as your health, your finances, or your family?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I had those bills I mentioned earlier, so I was certainly stressed about finances then, but... I don't spend my time just worrying about things. My health is fine, and my family is doing well. So, no, I don't really sit around worrying about everyday things like that.
Have you experienced any new physical symptoms, such as tremors, changes in your balance, or any unexplained sensations, since this restlessness began?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My balance is still good, and I don't have any shaking or... strange feelings. It's really just the restlessness, but physically, everything else seems perfectly fine.
When you feel this need to stay busy, is it because you have an uncomfortable, creeping, or crawling sensation in your legs that makes you feel like you have to move them?

No, it's not like that. I don't get any weird feelings in my legs, like crawling or anything uncomfortable. It's just... I just feel like I need to be doing something. It's not a physical ache or a strange sensation, just a general feeling of needing to keep moving.
Have you had any blood work or a physical examination recently where a doctor mentioned any issues with your thyroid or other metabolic functions?

No, I haven't heard anything about that. I mean, they draw my blood when I go in for my regular checkups, but my doctor has never mentioned any problems with my thyroid or... or my metabolism. As far as I know, all those tests have always come back perfectly fine.
When you feel this need to keep moving, do you often find that your muscles feel tight, tense, or sore, even if you aren't doing anything physically demanding?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My muscles don't feel tight or... or sore at all. They really feel perfectly fine. It's not a tense feeling in my body, it's just that I want to be up and doing something. But physically, my muscles aren't bothering me.
When you are trying to be still, do you feel an internal sense of nervousness or agitation that makes it difficult to relax, or is it more just a preference to keep your hands busy?

It's more of an internal feeling, I suppose. Like, when I'm at the senior center meetings, or... or sitting through the long announcements at church, I get this sort of ants-in-my-chair feeling. It's not just wanting to keep my hands busy, it's... I have to shift around in my seat, or maybe stand up to get a cup of coffee, or even just straighten up the papers in front of me just to get through it. It's hard to just sit completely still and relax.
When you have that 'ants-in-your-chair' feeling, do you also notice your heart racing, your palms sweating, or your breathing becoming faster?
No, I don't get any of that. My heart doesn't race, and I don't get sweaty or anything. It's really just the fidgeting and needing to move around. I don't feel panicked or out of breath.
Have you started taking any new medications, or changed the dosage of any of your existing medications, around the time this restlessness first began?

No, I haven't started anything new. I've been taking the exact same pills for a long time now, and... well, none of the dosages have changed either. So it's definitely not from any medication changes.
When you have this 'ants-in-your-chair' feeling, do you find that your mind is also racing with various thoughts, or is your mind relatively quiet while your body feels the need to move?

No, I wouldn't say my mind is racing. It's... well, it's relatively quiet. I'm usually just sitting there trying to pay attention to whatever is going on at the time. It's really just my body that feels like it needs to get up and go. My thoughts aren't spinning or anything like that, it's just that physical fidgety feeling.

Does this 'ants-in-your-chair' feeling happen only when you are in situations where you feel pressured to be productive, or does it also happen when you are completely alone at home with no tasks to complete?

I haven't really noticed a pattern like that, to be honest. I mean, I'm retired, so I don't have a lot of pressure to be productive these days anyway. But... I'm not really sure. It just sort of happens when I'm sitting down. I haven't kept track of whether it's worse when I have chores to do or if I'm just sitting by myself in the living room with nothing going on. It just happens.
When you have that feeling of needing to move, does it feel like an emotional discomfort or a sense of inner agitation, or is it strictly a physical sensation that you just need to move your body?

I'm not really sure how to separate the two, honestly. It's just... a feeling that I need to move. I don't think I feel emotionally upset or agitated, like angry or anxious, if that's what you mean. It's just a very strong, physical urge to get up or shift around. My body just doesn't want to stay still.
When you have this urge to move, does it feel like a distressing, unbearable tension that you are trying to escape, or is it more like a simple preference to be active?

Oh, I wouldn't call it unbearable. That sounds a bit too extreme. It's not a distressing tension that I'm trying to escape or anything like that. 

But... I don't know if I'd call it a simple preference, either. I mean, at my age, I'd often prefer to just sit and relax! It's really just... well, my body just decides it's done sitting and needs to shift around or stand up. I haven't really thought of it as either of those things, to be honest. It's just a physical urge that happens.
Does this feeling of needing to move around happen more often at certain times of the day, such as in the evening or at night?

I haven't really noticed it being tied to a specific time of day. It doesn't seem to happen more in the evening or at night, or anything like that. It just kind of happens whenever I've been sitting for a bit, whether it's morning or afternoon.

doctor.question: Does this feeling of needing to move around happen more often at certain times of the day, such as in the evening or at night?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about diurnal variation (specifically if the restlessness occurs more in the evening/night), which is often used to rule out Restless Legs Syndrome. The symptom profiles do not contain information about the time of day the symptoms occur.

patient.answer: I haven't really noticed it being tied to a specific time of day. It doesn't seem to happen more in the evening or at night, or anything like that. It just kind of happens whenever I've been sitting for a bit, whether it's morning or afternoon.

inference.note: The patient's clear denial of anxiety symptoms (heart racing, sweating, panic) and the absence of an unbearable/distressing tension (ruling out akathisia) makes F41.8 less likely, leaving the non-specific symptom of restlessness.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the patient's primary reason for seeking psychiatric consultation.
opening_question.question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent motor restlessness ('ants-in-the-chair' feeling) that does not meet the diagnostic criteria for anxiety disorders, restless legs syndrome, or medication-induced akathisia. Given the lack of psychiatric or neurological pathology, the symptoms are best classified as 'other symptoms and signs involving emotional state', specifically psychomotor restlessness.
